blocks.content: PART A: INTRODUCTION TO RBI

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The RBI was established on April 1, 1935, following the recommendations of the Hilton Young Commission.
RBI was nationalised on January 1, 1949, transforming it into a fully government-owned central bank.
Under Section 22 of the RBI Act 1934, RBI holds the sole right to issue currency notes in India, excluding one-rupee notes and coins.
Quantitative monetary tools like Repo Rate, CRR, SLR, and Open Market Operations are used to control credit and manage inflation.
Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) reserves must be kept as pure cash with the RBI, whereas Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) is maintained by banks with themselves in liquid assets.

blocks.content: 1. What is the Reserve Bank of India?

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the central bank of India. A central bank is the topmost monetary authority of a country. RBI controls the supply of money and credit in the Indian economy. It does not work for profit and does not deal directly with the general public.
RBI acts as the controller, regulator and supervisor of the entire banking system of India. All commercial banks work under the rules and guidelines issued by RBI.
2. Establishment of RBI

The Reserve Bank of India was established on 1 April 1935 under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. Initially, RBI was a private shareholders’ bank. In the year 1949, RBI was nationalised and came under government ownership.
3. Headquarters of RBI
The headquarters of the Reserve Bank of India is located in Mumbai, Maharashtra.
PART B: OBJECTIVES OF RBI (WHY RBI EXISTS)
4. Objectives of RBI (Explained One by One)

The main objectives of the Reserve Bank of India are:



• Price Stability – controlling inflation and deflation.

• Regulation of Money Supply – ensuring neither excess nor shortage of money.

• Control of Credit – regulating bank lending.

• Financial Stability – protecting banking system from failure.

• Economic Growth – supporting development policies of the government.
PART C: FUNCTIONS OF RBI (MOST IMPORTANT PART)
5. Issue of Currency
RBI has the sole authority to issue currency notes in India. All currency notes except one-rupee note are issued by RBI. One-rupee note and coins are issued by the Government of India.
This function ensures uniformity and trust in the currency system.
6. Banker to the Government
The Reserve Bank of India acts as the central monetary authority, regulating the credit system to maintain price stability and foster economic growth.
RBI acts as banker, agent and advisor to the Government of India. It receives and makes payments on behalf of the government and manages public debt.
7. Banker’s Bank
RBI acts as banker to commercial banks. Commercial banks keep a portion of their reserves with RBI. In times of financial difficulty, banks can borrow from RBI.
8. Custodian of Cash Reserves
RBI keeps the cash reserves of commercial banks in the form of CRR. This helps RBI control credit creation.
9. Controller of Credit (VERY IMPORTANT)
RBI controls credit creation and money supply in the economy through various monetary policy tools.
PART D: MONETARY POLICY OF RBI
10. Meaning of Monetary Policy

rows: Cash reserves deposited directly with RBI
Cash, Gold, or Approved Govt Securities kept with the bank itself
No interest is earned from RBI
Banks earn returns/yields on held securities
Controls excess money supply and liquidity in the banking system
Ensures bank liquidity/solvency and creates demand for government securities

blocks.content: Monetary policy refers to the policy of the central bank to regulate money supply and credit conditions in the economy in order to achieve price stability and growth.
11. Quantitative Tools of Credit Control
A. Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) – EXTREME DETAIL

CRR is the percentage of total deposits that commercial banks must keep as cash with the RBI. Banks cannot use this money for lending.



• Increase in CRR → less lending → controls inflation

• Decrease in CRR → more lending → promotes growth
B. Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) – EXTREME DETAIL

SLR is the percentage of deposits that banks must maintain in liquid assets such as cash, gold and government securities.



SLR ensures safety and solvency of banks.
C. Repo Rate – EXTREME DETAIL

Repo rate is the rate at which RBI lends short-term money to commercial banks against government securities.



• Increase in repo rate → loans become costly → inflation controlled

• Decrease in repo rate → loans become cheaper → growth encouraged
D. Reverse Repo Rate – EXTREME DETAIL
Reverse repo rate is the rate at which RBI borrows money from commercial banks. It helps RBI absorb excess liquidity.
E. Open Market Operations (OMO)

Open Market Operations refer to buying and selling of government securities by RBI in the open market.



• Buying securities → more money supply

• Selling securities → less money supply

items: The Hilton Young Commission (Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance, 1926) recommended the creation of the RBI.
One-rupee currency notes and coins are issued by the Ministry of Finance and bear the signature of the Finance Secretary, not the RBI Governor.
During inflationary periods, RBI hikes Repo Rate, CRR, and SLR to drain excess liquidity from the market.

blocks.content: PART E: EFFECT OF RBI TOOLS
12. Effect on Inflation and Growth
RBI uses CRR, SLR, Repo and OMO to control inflation and stabilize growth. Tight policy controls inflation; easy policy promotes growth.
PART F: ROLE OF RBI IN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
13. Developmental Role of RBI
RBI promotes economic development by regulating banks, ensuring financial inclusion, maintaining stability and supporting government policies.
SSC ABSOLUTE FINAL REVISION POINTS

• RBI is the central bank of India

• Established in 1935, nationalised in 1949

• Issues currency notes

• Controls credit through CRR, SLR, Repo

• Repo controls loan cost

• OMO controls liquidity
